passages.title: A label is not the parcel
passages.text: Imagine three parcels all labeled 7. Replacing one parcel’s label does not replace the others. A node is the parcel: an object with its own identity and fields. A value is a field’s current content. An address tells us where a node is stored. These three notions can coincide accidentally in a tiny example, but an implementation must not confuse them. In the scene, A, B, and C are identities, the labels are values, and the @ numbers are addresses. Duplicate values deliberately expose the distinction.

passages.title: A pointer encodes a relationship
passages.text: Let V be a finite set of live nodes and let addr: V → M injectively assign memory addresses. A successor field is an abstract function next: V → V ∪ {null}; its concrete pointer stores addr(next(v)) when a successor exists. Here null is a separate marker ∅, not an ordinary node. A machine could reserve address zero for it, but that is a representation convention. A raw pointer does not inherently know a node’s type, owner, or lifetime. Those constraints must come from the program’s contract.

passages.title: What must stay true
passages.text: At each completed operation, every nonnull pointer must designate a live node of the expected kind. That rule is necessary but not sufficient: a stale pointer can land on a newly allocated object at the same address. Object lifetime therefore matters as well as numeric address validity. The finite trace checks target existence and repairs addresses; it does not prove memory safety for arbitrary programs. When transferring this reasoning to a language with references, ask which parts the runtime enforces and which ownership rules the program still supplies.

passages.title: Ask what the program does often
passages.text: A list is an abstract ordered sequence before it is a memory layout. An array and a linked chain can represent the same identities in the same order. They differ in how the program reaches an element and changes the order. A useful design question is therefore specific: do we mostly ask for the kth element, scan all elements, insert beside a known node, or grow unpredictably? Without an operation mix, calling one representation faster hides the actual decision. The scene performs one identical last-element query under two layouts.

passages.title: Count only what the model counts
passages.text: Assume a random-access machine where arithmetic and reading one known address each cost a constant. An array computes the address of index k directly, then reads one data node. A singly linked chain starts at its head and follows k successor fields before it reads the kth node. Our displayed counter counts visited data nodes: one versus k+1. It excludes arithmetic, cache misses, pointer-field reads, and allocation. Naming the cost unit prevents an illustrative counter from being mistaken for a real elapsed-time measurement.

passages.title: A different operation changes the verdict
passages.text: Inserting after a known linked node can change a constant number of links, provided a free node is already available. Inserting at array position k while preserving order generally shifts n−k elements. But if only a value is given, finding the predecessor may dominate linked insertion. The phrase “known node” is an essential precondition, not a technicality. A linked node also needs link storage; an array may need spare capacity. Both representation cost and the search needed before an update belong in a fair comparison.

passages.title: The rule belongs to the ends
passages.text: A stack, queue, and deque can contain the same sequence of tokens yet permit different next operations. Fix left and right in the drawing. Here a stack inserts and removes on the right; a queue inserts right and removes left; an unrestricted deque allows insertion and deletion at either end. The word “top” identifies the stack’s chosen active end, not a direction in physical memory. Rotating a drawing cannot change the rule. These abstract interfaces work with either sequential or linked storage.

passages.text: Insert A, then B, then C. Removing from the stack returns C because C arrived most recently; removing from the queue returns A because A has waited longest. Our trace chooses left removal, then inserts Z at the left, an operation excluded from the chosen stack and queue interfaces. Each token keeps its identity across the transition so that an exit cannot be confused with a relabeling.

passages.title: Why the order laws hold
passages.text: A stack removal selects the last surviving insertion at its active end; that is last-in, first-out. A queue removal selects the earliest insertion not yet removed; that is first-in, first-out. Induction on a legal operation history proves these statements: insertion establishes a new last element and deletion removes the specified endpoint without changing the others’ relative order. Our finite model compares resulting sequences, but the induction explains arbitrary histories. Neither law says what scheduling policy is fair when new operations keep arriving forever.

passages.title: Pending work is part of the algorithm
passages.text: Suppose visiting a task reveals smaller tasks that should be done later. The pending structure determines what “later” means. A queue keeps tasks in discovery order and therefore finishes the current tree level before the next. A stack returns to the most recently saved task, producing a depth-first route. The scene uses a fixed rooted tree and the same children in both runs. We reverse the push order for a stack so that the left child is visited first; otherwise an unnoticed implementation detail would reverse siblings.

passages.title: Follow the frontier, not just the route
passages.text: After A is visited, B and C are pending. Queue scheduling takes B and then C before B’s children; stack scheduling takes B and proceeds through B’s descendants while C waits. The frontier is not a picture of all unvisited vertices: it contains only discovered tasks that have not yet been processed. Vertices can exist in the input without having entered that frontier. Watching both the highlighted tree vertex and the pending sequence explains the route causally rather than asking the learner to memorize the names breadth-first and depth-first.

passages.title: Discovery needs its own bookkeeping
passages.text: On a tree, each nonroot vertex has exactly one parent, so discovering the same vertex twice is impossible. On a general graph, two parents may point to the same vertex, or a cycle may return to an ancestor. Mark a vertex when it is scheduled, not only after it is processed, if the policy is to enqueue each identity once. Maintain a set D of discovered vertices and admit child u only when u∉D. Without this extra state, changing the container alone does not make a safe graph traversal.

passages.title: State what the order guarantees
passages.text: For an unweighted graph, queue discovery produces nondecreasing shortest-path distance from the start when every edge is considered and vertices are marked on discovery. passages.title: Check before an invalid memory access
passages.text: When T=M, there is no slot T, so push must reject before writing. When T=0, decrementing would produce −1, so pop must reject before changing T. passages.title: Prove order through the representation map
passages.text: The representation map reads n cells starting at h around the ring. A legal enqueue adds a value exactly after its current last mapped cell because t≡h+n. A legal dequeue removes exactly its first mapped cell by advancing h. Both preserve the congruence and the FIFO sequence. This proof works for M=1 too, where head and tail are always equal and count carries all state distinction. It assumes sequential operations; publishing indices safely between concurrent producers and consumers requires a separate memory-ordering argument.

passages.title: Let two tables borrow the same slack
passages.text: Giving two stacks separate fixed capacities can fail one stack while unused cells remain in the other region. Instead place one stack at the low end of a shared area and another at the high end. Let L be the first unused cell after the left stack and R the first occupied cell of the right stack. Their occupied intervals are [0,L) and [R,M); the shared gap is [L,R). Only the total occupancy determines whether another push fits.

passages.title: Opposite growth makes collision simple
passages.text: A left push writes at L and increments L. A right push decrements R and writes at R. Both first require L<R. The scene alternates pushes until the boundary indices meet; the next attempted push is rejected without changing a value. Every slot has a visible role: left-owned, right-owned, or unused. This is stronger than counting total elements alone because it states exactly where each owner may write. A left pop and a right pop reverse their respective endpoint updates.

passages.title: More tables require a relocation policy
passages.text: Three or more independently growing contiguous tables cannot all enjoy the simple two-ended arrangement. A manager may move a table into a larger gap and adjust its base address. If source and destination overlap, movement order matters: moving a block to higher addresses requires copying from its high end downward, while moving lower requires copying low to high. Otherwise a write can destroy an unread source item. A temporary buffer is another correct solution. Raw external pointers also need repair when a table relocates.

passages.title: Unused cells can form a list too
passages.text: Linked structures need a way to obtain a node when inserting data. Put unused fixed-size slots on a free list whose head is AVAIL. Allocation removes its first slot; recycling pushes a retired slot back. The links inside free slots have allocator meaning, while links inside live nodes have data-structure meaning. A slot cannot safely serve both roles at once. In the partition formula, P means all pool slots, L the live slots, R the reserved slots, and F the free slots. The dotted union symbol ⊎ means these sets do not overlap. Our three-rail scene makes a normally hidden state explicit: a reserved slot belongs to an in-progress operation until it is initialized and published.

passages.title: Separate reservation from publication
passages.text: Allocation first checks AVAIL≠null. It reads the free head p, advances AVAIL to p’s former successor, and takes ownership of p. The program then initializes p’s value and live successor before making a live predecessor or head point to p. Publishing first could expose an uninitialized link. Each frame checks that the universe of slots is exactly partitioned into live, reserved, and free sets. At completed operation boundaries the reserved set is empty; during a multi-step update it accounts for otherwise missing storage.

passages.title: Unlink before recycling
passages.text: Deletion first removes every live route by which the structure owns the node, then retires it, then gives its slot to the allocator. Recycling while a live link still points there would let the same address belong to unrelated logical structures. The example allocates two nodes, removes one, and reuses its slot for M. The numeric address repeats, but the old object lifetime does not. An external pointer to the former object is stale even if the slot now contains a valid new node.

passages.title: Conservation catches concrete mistakes
passages.text: A lost slot violates coverage of the pool; double allocation or double free violates disjointness. These are checkable invariants over finite slot identities, not assumptions about their labels. A full free list is not required: it may be empty when every slot is live. Allocation must then fail or invoke a separately specified recovery policy. The fixed-size model does not address fragmentation, variable-size allocation, tracing reachability from arbitrary roots, or concurrent reclamation. Those topics require additional state beyond this useful first conservation law.

passages.title: Two endpoints save a traversal
passages.text: A linked queue keeps a head h for removal and a tail t for insertion. The live successor chain runs from h to t, and next(t)=null. An empty nonsentinel queue has both endpoints null. The tail avoids scanning the chain on every enqueue, but it creates an invariant that must be maintained together with the head. In contrast, a linked stack needs only its top: insertion and removal both modify that same end. Neither interface implies that nodes are consecutive in memory.

passages.title: Handle the first and last nodes explicitly
passages.text: To enqueue a new initialized node p, set next(p)=null. If the queue is empty, set both h and t to p; otherwise link the former tail to p and then update t. To dequeue, reject an empty queue, save the head’s value, and advance h to next(h). If h becomes null, set t to null too. Forgetting that final update leaves a dangling tail after removing the last node. Our trace empties and refills the structure specifically to expose this boundary.

passages.title: A sentinel changes the empty convention
passages.text: A dummy header can make the head node always present, with real data beginning at its successor. In one common queue design, tail equals the header when no data remain. That does not mean the queue contains a data item: the sentinel is administrative storage. Sentinel and nonsentinel formulas must not be mixed. Our executable scene uses no sentinel; the circular-list lesson will make a sentinel visible. For a stack, a new node can point to the old top before the top pointer is changed.

passages.title: Constraints are directed edges
passages.text: A precedence constraint u→v says u must appear before v. A topological ordering lists every vertex once while respecting every edge. passages.title: An empty queue is not always success
passages.text: If the ready queue empties and R is empty, the ordering is complete. If R is nonempty, every remaining vertex has an incoming edge from another remaining vertex. passages.title: Correctness and cost use different arguments
passages.text: Every emitted vertex has no remaining prerequisite, so appending it cannot place it before an unprocessed predecessor. Induction proves the output prefix respects all constraints. In an acyclic nonempty residual graph, the predecessor-following argument rules out all positive counts, so another ready vertex exists. Here V is the vertex set, E the directed edge set, T the amount of work, and S the storage required; |V| and |E| count their members. With adjacency lists, each vertex enters and leaves the queue once and each edge causes one decrement, giving O(|V|+|E|) work. The explicit cycle witness uses extra traversal only on failure; the source’s count-based method and our small witness extension are distinguished.

passages.title: Closing the chain changes the stopping rule
passages.text: A circular list replaces the final null successor with a link back into the structure. Every node therefore has a successor, and repeated traversal never encounters null. A list can be represented by a pointer to one data node, stopping when that identity returns, or by a distinguished sentinel H. Here H is permanent administrative storage and next(H)=H represents an empty data list. The sentinel must be recognized by identity or an unambiguous tag, never merely by a data value that might also occur in a real node.

passages.title: Multiplication creates contributions, then combines them
passages.text: A term cx^e times dx^f contributes cd·x^(e+f). Different term pairs can produce the same exponent, so the grid of pairwise products is not yet a canonical output list. The model accumulates contributions by exponent, deleting a key whenever its exact coefficient becomes zero. This is the algebraic equivalent of repeatedly merging scaled, exponent-shifted copies of a polynomial into an accumulator. In several variables, exponents become vectors and multiplication adds them componentwise under a chosen consistent monomial ordering.

passages.title: Cancellation changes storage, not just a label
passages.text: If a coefficient becomes zero, retaining its node violates our sparse representation convention. Deleting it must preserve list links and recycle storage correctly in a linked implementation; the model’s map removes the corresponding term identity. Exact integer arithmetic makes equality to zero unambiguous. Approximate coefficients would need a deliberately chosen numerical policy and would no longer satisfy the same canonical equality rule automatically. Evaluation at finitely many sample x values helps catch mistakes but is not, by itself, a proof that arbitrary symbolic polynomials are equal.

passages.title: Each neighboring relation has two fields
passages.text: In a doubly linked list, next(v) points forward and prev(v) points backward. For every published node v, the neighboring fields must agree: prev(next(v))=v and next(prev(v))=v. They do not tell us which list owns an arbitrary node or whether it is already retired.

passages.title: Choose the level where an invariant holds
passages.text: An invariant may describe public operation boundaries without holding after each individual instruction. passages.title: Advance to the next change
passages.text: A discrete-event simulation represents changes scheduled at particular simulated times. Between consecutive event times, a system state may remain constant, so incrementing a clock through every unused tick wastes effort and can obscure the model. Our original workshop has arriving jobs, one tool, and a FIFO waiting line. An arrival may begin service immediately or wait; a completion releases the tool and may schedule another completion. Write ℰ for the set of future events and t(e) for event e’s scheduled time. The minimum over ℰ chooses the next event time. The event calendar holds future changes, while the waiting line holds entities awaiting a resource. They are different structures.

passages.title: Statistics belong to intervals
passages.text: Let W be the accumulated waiting-time area, measured in job-time units. If q jobs wait throughout [t_old,t_new), add q(t_new−t_old) to the waiting-time area before applying the event at t_new. Using the queue length after the event would charge a job for time it did not wait or fail to charge one that just left. The model records this area exactly with integer times and compares it against an independent per-job waiting calculation. Busy time, queueing time, and turnaround time are different quantities and should never share a label merely because each involves the clock.

passages.title: An index tuple is a mixed-radix number
passages.text:
Let d≥1 be the number of axes, with positive integer lengths n₁,…,n_d. Coordinate i_t has the half-open domain ℓ_t≤i_t<ℓ_t+n_t. Subtract its lower bound to obtain digit δ_t=i_t−ℓ_t, so 0≤δ_t<n_t. In row-major order the last digit changes fastest. Increasing digit t by one skips every possible combination of later digits: its stride is the product of n_u for u>t. The empty product for the last axis equals 1. Summing each digit times its stride gives the offset k; a c-unit record at base b begins at b+ck. The source’s inclusive zero-based upper bounds d_t correspond to our lengths n_t=d_t+1.

For shape 2×2×3, the strides are 6,3,1: one plane contains six slots and one row contains three. Our selected coordinates (3,0,6), with lower bounds (2,−1,4), become digits (1,1,2). They select one plane, then one row, then its third slot. The same calculation can be evaluated without building a stride table: start h₀=0 and set h_t=h_{t−1}n_t+δ_t. This trace computes 1, then 3, then offset 11, retaining the same cell identities while the planes flatten.

Invert from the last axis backward. Repeated division with remainder by n_d,n_{d−1},…,n₁ recovers each digit; add its lower bound to recover the coordinate. Here divmod(11,3)=(3,2), divmod(3,2)=(1,1), and divmod(1,2)=(0,1). The unique remainder at each step proves uniqueness, while repeated quotient reduction recovers a valid tuple for every 0≤k<∏n_t. Thus the map is a bijection for arbitrary positive dimensions; exhaustive finite tests check the implementation rather than replace this argument. An axis of length 1 is valid and contributes only digit zero. Empty or invalid dimensions and out-of-range coordinates are rejected.

passages.title: Zeros need not occupy data nodes
passages.text: A sparse matrix can store only nonzero entries. Each stored cell has a row, a column, a value, and enough links to join its row list and column list. Maintaining separate copied values in unrelated row and column structures would introduce a synchronization problem: an update could change one copy but not the other. In our diagram horizontal and vertical routes meet at one circle with one identity, while absent positions have the precise implied value zero. The source uses circular lists with header nodes and LEFT/UP links traversing decreasing coordinates. This teaching diagram instead shows routes in increasing row/column order without drawing circular return links. Shared cell identity and membership are preserved, but these arrows are not a literal rendering of the source’s link orientation.

passages.title: Preserve operands until their last use
passages.text: Let A be the original matrix and B the changing output matrix. The pivot is at row p and column q, so a=A[p,q]. passages.title: Exactness and numerical stability are different questions
passages.text: Fractions preserve exact cancellation, so equality to zero is decisive here. Floating-point implementations must address rounding, small pivots, and an explicit sparsity policy; substituting a tolerance is an algorithmic choice with consequences. A zero pivot is rejected before any mutation. Independent tests evaluate the four-case formula directly on small matrices and compare every final entry, including negative and fractional pivots. Those tests establish evidence for this implementation, not numerical stability of a larger solver or correctness of an entire matrix-inversion procedure.
